opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I care a lot about.

When we talk about intelligence, we often focus on the parts that are easy to measure: recognizing objects, answering questions, writing code, winning games. Those are real achievements. But human intelligence has never been only about solving problems. A huge part of it is social and emotional: understanding what another person needs, reading context, knowing when to speak and when to listen, sensing when something matters deeply to someone.

That matters for AI right now because these systems are no longer sitting in a lab. They're in classrooms, hospitals, and homes. They're talking to people who may be lonely, sick, anxious, or vulnerable. If a system is technically brilliant but blind to the human on the other side, it can be unhelpful at best and harmful at worst. Think of a patient getting a frightening diagnosis, or an elderly person living alone, or a child who's struggling. Getting the facts right is necessary, but it isn't sufficient. How you show up for that person matters enormously.

I want to be careful here, though. I don't think we should pretend machines feel things the way we do, and I'm wary of systems built to simulate empathy in order to manipulate or maximize engagement. That's the wrong goal. What I mean by emotional intelligence in AI is closer to awareness and respect: systems that recognize human states and context, respond appropriately, and are designed to support human dignity and agency rather than exploit our emotions.

This goes back to what I've always believed about human-centered AI. The point of the technology is to augment people, not replace them or diminish them. You can't really augment a human if you don't understand what it means to be human, and emotion is a central part of that. So for me, emotional intelligence isn't a nice-to-have feature on top of capability. It's part of what makes AI trustworthy and beneficial.

r001.rationale: The response says AI should recognize human states and context, but does not suggest theory of mind as a route to emotional intelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes AI being used in everyday settings and the risks of poor responses, but does not raise concern that people already depend too much on AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, it's a pleasure to be here.

I think emotional intelligence matters because, at its core, AI is not really about machines. It's about people. When I started working on ImageNet, the question I was asking was not "how do we make computers see?" in the abstract. It was "how do we give machines the kind of visual understanding that lets them be useful in a human world?" And a human world is full of emotion, context, and nuance that a bounding box simply doesn't capture.

If you think about where AI is being deployed today, it's in hospitals, in classrooms, in homes with aging parents. I spent years working on ambient intelligence in healthcare, watching how nurses and caregivers move through a room. What struck me was how much of their expertise is emotional. They notice when a patient is anxious before any vital sign changes. They adjust their tone. A system that can recognize a fall but cannot sense a person's dignity is only half a system, and maybe the less important half.

So when I say emotional intelligence matters, I mean two things. First, the technology itself needs to model and respect human states, not just human objects. Second, and honestly more important, the people building AI need emotional intelligence. We need to understand the fears of the communities our tools will touch, the hopes of the students who will inherit this field, the real stakes for workers whose jobs will change. That's why I keep coming back to the phrase "human-centered AI." It's not a slogan to me. It's a discipline. It means asking, at every step, who is this for, and how will it make them feel about their own agency.

The history of technology tells us that the most transformative tools are the ones that augment human capability rather than replace human judgment. Emotional intelligence is what keeps us on the right side of that line.

r001.rationale: The response discusses modeling and respecting human states, but does not mention theory of mind as a route to AI emotional intelligence.

r002.rationale: It argues that AI should augment rather than replace human judgment, but does not raise concern that people may already depend too much on AI.

astra-6.text:
I think emotional intelligence matters because intelligence is not just about solving a mathematical problem or recognizing an object. It’s also about understanding people—their needs, their intentions, and the context in which they’re asking for help.

Imagine an AI system assisting an older adult at home. Getting a task right is important, but so is recognizing when that person is confused or uncomfortable, and responding respectfully. That requires more than technical accuracy.

This doesn’t mean we should assume machines have feelings. We need to distinguish between experiencing emotion and responding appropriately to human emotion. And we should be humble: even people misunderstand one another. For AI, sometimes the most appropriate response is to ask a question rather than assume it knows how someone feels.

Ultimately, if we want AI to benefit people, we have to take the human experience seriously.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding people’s needs, intentions, and context, but does not suggest theory of mind as a route to emotional intelligence in AI.

r002.rationale: It does not raise concern that people may already depend too much on AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think emotional intelligence matters because intelligence is not just about solving an equation or recognizing an object. In our lives, intelligence is deeply connected to understanding people—their intentions, their needs, and the context they’re in.

Imagine an AI system helping an older adult at home. It might correctly recognize every object in the room, but if it cannot recognize that the person is confused or distressed, it may miss the most important thing happening.

That doesn’t mean the machine has to feel emotions. We should be careful about that distinction. But it does need to respond appropriately to people, with an awareness of uncertainty and respect for their agency. For me, that is part of building human-centered AI: asking not only what a technology can do, but how it can help people.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding people’s intentions, needs, and context, but does not suggest that theory of mind could provide a route to emotional intelligence in AI.
